title: Sikhism: remembering the name
hookLine: remembering God through the name, in breath and song

cards: Long before sunrise in Amritsar, the city is dark, but the Golden Temple is lit up, its reflection shivering on the water around it.

People are already walking the marble path barefoot, and from inside comes music: a harmonium, small drums, voices singing verses from the scripture. It goes on, in shifts, almost all day. Some of the walkers sing along.
Some are silent, lips barely moving, repeating a single word.

teach.b: Naam means the name. In Sikh teaching it's more than a label: it's the presence of the one creator, yesterday's Ik Onkar, running through everything.
Simran means remembering. So naam simran is remembering the name, keeping the one close until the mind is steeped in it.
Sikh tradition counts it the first of three pillars of Sikh life, taught by Guru Nanak; the other two, honest work and sharing, come in the next two days. How is it done?
Sikhs often repeat Waheguru, a Sikh name for God often explained as wonderful Lord, or wondrous teacher, silently or aloud, sometimes with the breath: wahe on the in-breath, guru on the out-breath.
Some rise in the hours before dawn, called amrit vela, the ambrosial time, to bathe, recite Japji and sit in simran before the day starts. And much of it is sung.
The Guru Granth Sahib is written almost entirely as poetry set to musical modes called raags, and kirtan, singing it, fills the gurdwara.
A line in the Sukhmani Sahib, by the fifth Guru, Arjan, says in effect: remember, remember, remember, and find peace. The Gurus taught this wasn't escape from the world.
Guru Nanak compared a person living with the name to a lotus that grows in muddy water yet isn't stained by it.
The idea is to keep the name while living a full, busy life, not instead of one.

how: Many Sikhs rise at amrit vela before dawn to recite Japji and meditate on Waheguru, join kirtan in the gurdwara, and repeat the name quietly through the day.

o: reading the whole scripture in one sitting
chanting a secret word given by a teacher
keeping God in mind through the name

games.q: remembering the name — tap the pairs.
p: the name, the presence of the one

s: naam simran means leaving the world to meditate
Guru Nanak's lotus grows in muddy water: remember the name within a full life.
the Guru Granth Sahib is written almost entirely as poetry set to music
arranged by musical modes called raags.
naam simran is the first of three pillars of Sikh life

games.q: you want to keep God in mind all day, but you have a job and a family. what did Guru Nanak teach?
o: leave everything and live in a forest.
live fully in the world, remembering the name, like a lotus in muddy water.
games.why: the Gurus taught simran within ordinary life, not instead of it: the lotus isn't stained by the mud.

practice: Borrowed from kirtan: breathe in, and on the out-breath let one low, easy note hum in your chest.

If you're Sikh, you might let Waheguru ride on the note; if not, the hum alone is enough, or any word that points you toward what matters. When thoughts come, let them float like the lotus on the water, and come back to the sound.

wordCard.voice: Naam simran. Remembering the name: keeping the one creator in mind, in breath and song, through a busy day. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the name. In breath, in song, in the hours before dawn. See you tomorrow.
